1.q: אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָיָ֧ה דְבַר יְהוָ֛ה אֶל יִרְמְיָ֥הוּ הַ⁠נָּבִ֖יא עַל הַ⁠גּוֹיִֽם
1.note: Jeremiah is using the heading **The word of Yahweh that was to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations** to introduce a new section of the book. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new section.
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:9.
See how you translated the similar expression in 35:12.

2.q: פַּרְעֹ֤ה נְכוֹ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ מִצְרַ֔יִם אֲשֶׁר הָיָ֥ה עַל נְהַר פְּרָ֖ת בְּ⁠כַרְכְּמִ֑שׁ
2.note: The word **Neco** is the name of a man, **Euphrates** is the name of a river, and **Carchemish** is the name of a city.

2.q: אֲשֶׁר הָיָ֥ה עַל נְהַר פְּרָ֖ת בְּ⁠כַרְכְּמִ֑שׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִכָּ֗ה נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ בָּבֶ֔ל בִּ⁠שְׁנַת֙ הָֽ⁠רְבִיעִ֔ית לִ⁠יהוֹיָקִ֥ים בֶּן יֹאשִׁיָּ֖הוּ מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה
2.note: Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand the message that follows. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Here, **Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon** represents “the army of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [which the army of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck]
See how you translated this phrase in [25:1](ta:25).

3.note: A **small shield** was a kind of light, round shield that a soldier held in one hand, and a **large shield** was a kind of shield big enough to cover most of a soldier’s body. If your readers would not be familiar with these kinds of shields, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [light round shields and full-body shields]

4.note: The **helmets** were hard coverings that soldiers wore to protect their heads, and the **body armor** was a covering of metal plates or rings that soldiers wore to protect their bodies. If your readers would not be familiar with these things, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [with hard head coverings … the metal body coverings]

5.note: The word “I” here refers to Yahweh. Yahweh uses a question to introduce the vision and to draw attention to what he says next. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation as in the UST.
The pronoun **They** refers to the soldiers of Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The Egyptian soldiers are dismayed, turning back backward]

The expression **are crushed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the soldiers of Babylon. Alternate translation: [and the soldiers of Babylon have crushed their mighty ones]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and a noun come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

The implication is that the soldiers of Egypt did not turn around to face their enemies and fight them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they have not turned around to fight their enemies]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:25.
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8.

The word “I” here refers to Yahweh. Yahweh uses a question to introduce the vision and to draw attention to what he says next. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation as in the UST.

6.q: אַל יָנ֣וּס הַ⁠קַּ֔ל וְ⁠אַל יִמָּלֵ֖ט הַ⁠גִּבּ֑וֹר
6.note: Yahweh is using the adjectives **swift** and **mighty** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [The soldiers who run fast cannot flee, and the mighty soldier cannot escape]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the soldiers of Egypt were people who **stumble** and **fall** down. It means that they will be defeated and killed in battle. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are defeated and they die]

7.note: By **the streams**, Yahweh means the streams that branch off from the Nile River and would overflow at the time of year when the Nile River was at flood stage. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [like the streams of the Nile River at flood stage]

7.q: מִי זֶ֖ה כַּ⁠יְאֹ֣ר יַֽעֲלֶ֑ה כַּ⁠נְּהָר֕וֹת יִֽתְגָּעֲשׁ֖וּ מֵימָֽי⁠ו
7.note: Yahweh is using the question form to introduce the army of Egypt in a dramatic way. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Look at this army rising up like the Nile, like the streams whose waters surge back and forth!]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the Nile** and **the streams** rise up and spread over the land when their waters surge, so the army of Egypt is advancing and spreading over the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [rising up and spreading over the land like the Nile does, like the streams do when their waters surge back and forth]
The word **Nile** is the name of a river, the main river in Egypt.

8.note: Here, **Egypt** represents “the army of Egypt.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The Egyptian army rises up like the Nile]

8.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֗אמֶר אַֽעֲלֶה֙ אֲכַסֶּה אֶ֔רֶץ אֹבִ֥ידָה עִ֖יר וְ⁠יֹ֥שְׁבֵי בָֽ⁠הּ
8.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And he said that he would rise, that he would cover the earth, and that he would destroy the city and the dwellers in it]

The army of Egypt says **let me cover the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Let me rise, let me conquer many lands]

The army of Egypt is not referring to a specific **city**. It means cities in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any city and the people who live in it]

9.note: Here, **horses** represents “the men riding on horses,” and **chariots** represents “the men driving chariots.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Go up, O horsemen, and drive madly O charioteers]

9.q: כּ֤וּשׁ וּ⁠פוּט֙ תֹּפְשֵׂ֣י מָגֵ֔ן וְ⁠לוּדִ֕ים תֹּפְשֵׂ֖י
9.note: The words **Cush**, **Put**, and **Lud** are the names of people groups.

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [ones grasping the bow, ones treading the bow]

Yahweh is using **ones treading the bow** as a common expression of the culture to mean “ones who bend the bow and shoot arrows.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [ones who shoot arrows with the bow]

10.q: And the sword will devour and be satisfied and be quenched from their blood
10.note: Yahweh is speaking of **the sword** as if it were a living thing that could eat and **be satisfied** and drink and have its thirst **quenched**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the swords of the warriors will kill many men]

10.q: וְֽ⁠הַ⁠יּ֨וֹם הַ⁠ה֜וּא לַ⁠אדֹנָ֧⁠י יְהוִ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת י֤וֹם נְקָמָה֙
10.note: The implication is that **that day** of battle belongs to Yahweh because it is the day when he will punish his enemies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And that day of battle belongs to Lord Yahweh of Armies, because it is the day when he will punish his enemies]

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a day when he will pay back his enemies for what they have done]

Here, **the sword** represents “the enemy soldiers who fight with swords.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the soldiers with their swords]

The terms **be satisfied** and **be quenched** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and be completely satisfied]

10.q: זֶ֠בַח לַ⁠אדֹנָ֨⁠י יְהוִ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת בְּ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ צָפ֖וֹן
10.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the soldiers of Egypt who will die in battle were a **sacrifice** offered to him. It means that Yahweh will cause many of them to be killed as his punishment on them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Lord Yahweh of Armies will cause many soldiers to be killed as punishment in the land of the north]
See how you translated this name in 2:19.
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:22.

11.note: The phrase **I have multiplied** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [you have multiplied]

The commands **Go up** and **take** are singular here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Egypt as if they were one woman, the **virgin daughter of Egypt**. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He tells Egypt to go and get medicine, but he means that no medicine will be able to heal her. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Even if you go up to Gilead and take balm, it will not help you]
See how you translated this word in 8:22.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Egypt were a **virgin daughter**. It means that, just as a virgin had never been with a man, Egypt had never been conquered by an enemy. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O people of Egypt, whom no enemy has ever conquered]

Yahweh is using **For emptiness** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in vain.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [To no purpose]
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:13.

12.note: Here, **your shame** represents “the report of how you have been shamed.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The nations have heard the report of how you have been shamed]

Yahweh says **your cry has filled the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and people in many lands have heard you crying loudly]

12.q: גִבּ֤וֹר בְּ⁠גִבּוֹר֙ כָּשָׁ֔לוּ יַחְדָּ֖יו נָפְל֥וּ שְׁנֵי⁠הֶֽם
12.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [mighty soldiers have tripped over one another and have all fallen down together]

The pronoun **them** refers to the two mighty soldiers who stumbled against each other. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [together both mighty soldiers have fallen]

13.q: הַ⁠דָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר דִּבֶּ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה אֶֽל יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ הַ⁠נָּבִ֑יא
13.note: Jeremiah is using the heading **The word that Yahweh spoke to Jeremiah the prophet** to introduce a new section of the book. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new section.

If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **coming**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [regarding how Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon was going to come]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:3.
See how you translated the similar expression in 35:12.

14.note: The expression **cause it to be heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and tell it to the people in Migdol]
The word **Migdol** is the name of a city in Egypt.

14.q: אִמְר֗וּ הִתְיַצֵּב֙ וְ⁠הָכֵ֣ן לָ֔⁠ךְ כִּֽי אָכְלָ֥ה חֶ֖רֶב סְבִיבֶֽי⁠ךָ
14.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tell them to station themselves and prepare themselves, for a sword will devour those around them]

Here, **a sword** represents “enemy soldiers who fight with swords.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [enemy soldiers will devour those around you]
See how you translated this name in 2:16.

15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize how completely the soldiers of Egypt have been defeated. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Your mighty ones have been completely cut down!]

The expression **been cut down** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Why has Yahweh cut down your mighty ones]

This could mean: (1) the phrase **your mighty ones** refers to the warriors of Egypt (2) the phrase **your mighty ones** refers to Apis, the bull god that the Egyptians worshiped. The word translated as **mighty ones** can also mean “bulls,” the verbs that follow are singular in the original language, and some ancient versions understand this as a reference to Apis. Alternate translation: [your mighty warriors]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the soldiers of Egypt were people who **did not stand** on their feet. It means that they were not able to resist their enemies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They were not able to resist their enemies]

16.q: הִרְבָּ֖ה כּוֹשֵׁ֑ל גַּם נָפַ֞ל אִ֣ישׁ אֶל רֵעֵ֗⁠הוּ
16.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the soldiers of Egypt were people **stumbling** and falling down. It means that they are being defeated and killed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He caused many to be defeated; yes, one soldier has been killed alongside another]

This could mean: (1) the pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh, who caused many soldiers of Egypt to stumble (2) the pronoun **He** does not refer to a specific person, and the phrase means that many soldiers kept stumbling. Alternate translation: [Yahweh caused many soldiers to stumble]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **man**. He means soldiers in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [soldiers have fallen upon one another]

16.q: וַ⁠יֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ ק֣וּמָ⁠ה וְ⁠נָשֻׁ֣בָה אֶל עַמֵּ֗⁠נוּ וְ⁠אֶל אֶ֨רֶץ֙ מֽוֹלַדְתֵּ֔⁠נוּ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֖י חֶ֥רֶב הַ⁠יּוֹנָֽה
16.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And they said to one another that they should get up and return to their people and to the land of their birth, from the face of the sword of the oppressor]

The soldiers are using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “away from.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [away from the sword of the oppressor]

17.q: קָרְא֖וּ שָׁ֑ם פַּרְעֹ֤ה מֶֽלֶךְ מִצְרַ֨יִם֙ שָׁא֔וֹן הֶעֱבִ֖יר הַ⁠מּוֹעֵֽד
17.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [There they call out that Pharaoh king of Egypt is a loud noise and that he has let the appointed time pass by]

This could mean: (1) the people are speaking as if Pharaoh were nothing but **a loud noise**. They mean that he boasts loudly but is not able to do what he says (2) the people are giving Pharaoh a mocking name, “Loud Noise,” because his boasting came to nothing. Alternate translation: [Pharaoh king of Egypt only makes empty boasts]

The people are using **he has let the appointed time to pass by** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he has missed his opportunity.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has missed his opportunity]

18.note: See how you translated this phrase in 22:24.

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **the King, Yahweh of Armies**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, the King, declare this, and my name is Yahweh of Armies]
See how you translated this expression in 31:35.

The point of this comparison is that just as **Tabor** stands high **among the mountains** and **Carmel** stands high **by the sea**, so the king who **will come** against Egypt will be much more powerful than those around him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will come, standing as far above others as Tabor stands above the mountains and as Carmel stands above the sea]
The word **Tabor** is the name of a mountain.

The pronoun **he** refers to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will come to attack Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon will come]

19.note: The implication is that the people of Egypt should pack the few things that they can carry, because enemies will take them away as captives. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Pack a few things you can carry for yourself, because enemies will take you away into exile]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for Memphis will become completely empty and ruined]

The expression **it will be burned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the enemy soldiers. Alternate translation: [and enemy soldiers will set it on fire]

Yahweh says **without a dweller** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [with hardly anyone living there]

20.note: The enemy army coming to attack the Egyptians is spoken of as if the army were an insect that stings. Alternate translation: [but a powerful army like a stinging insect]
A **gadfly** is a kind of stinging fly. If your readers would not be familiar with what a gadfly is, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a stinging fly]

Yahweh is repeating the word **beautiful** and the word **coming** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification as in the UST.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if Egypt were a **beautiful, beautiful heifer**. It means that Egypt is a beautiful and prosperous nation. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Egypt is a very beautiful and prosperous nation]

Yahweh is repeating the word **beautiful** and the word **coming** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification as in the UST.

21.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **calves of the stall** are well fed but will soon be slaughtered, so are the soldiers whom Egypt has hired. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Also her hired ones among her are well fed but will soon be slaughtered, like calves of the stall]

The implication is that **her hired ones** are foreign soldiers whom Egypt paid to fight for her. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [her mercenary soldiers whom she paid to fight among her]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:12.
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:17.

22.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a serpent** makes only a quiet hissing sound as it **goes away**, so the people of Egypt will make only a faint sound as they flee. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As she flees, she makes only a quiet hissing sound, like a serpent that slips away]
The pronoun **they** refers to the enemy soldiers who are attacking Egypt. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for in force the enemy soldiers go]

The point of this comparison is that just as **men cutting down trees** come with **axes** to chop down a forest, so the enemy soldiers will come to cut down the people of Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and with axes they have come against her to cut down her people, just as men cut down trees]

23.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the people of Egypt were a **forest** that enemies have cut down. It means that the enemies will kill many of the people of Egypt. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have killed her many people]

The expression **it will not be searched out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one can search through it]

This could mean: (1) the forest of Egypt is so dense that no one could go through it, yet the enemy will still cut it down (2) the enemy soldiers are so many that no one could count them. Alternate translation: [it is so dense that no one can pass through it]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the locust** comes in swarms too large to count, so the enemy soldiers are too many to count. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the enemy soldiers are as numerous as a huge swarm of locusts]

Yahweh says **there is no number to them** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and they are extremely numerous]

24.note: The expression **will be put to shame** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The people of the north will put the daughter of Egypt to shame]

The expression **she will be given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will give her into the hand of the people of the north]

Here, **hand** represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the control of the people of the north]

25.note: The term **says** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

Yahweh is using **visiting punishment upon** as a common expression of the culture to mean “punishing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Behold me, bringing punishment upon Amon from No]
The word **Amon** is the name of a god, and **No** is the name of a city in Egypt.

25.q: וְ⁠עַל פַּרְעֹה֙ וְ⁠עַל מִצְרַ֔יִם וְ⁠עַל אֱלֹהֶ֖י⁠הָ וְ⁠עַל מְלָכֶ֑י⁠הָ וְ⁠עַ֨ל פַּרְעֹ֔ה וְ⁠עַ֥ל הַ⁠בֹּטְחִ֖ים בּֽ⁠וֹ
25.note: Yahweh uses a repetitive series of clauses to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

26.q: בְּ⁠יַד֙ מְבַקְשֵׁ֣י נַפְשָׁ֔⁠ם וּ⁠בְ⁠יַ֛ד נְבֽוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֥ר מֶֽלֶךְ בָּבֶ֖ל וּ⁠בְ⁠יַד עֲבָדָ֑י⁠ו
26.note: Here, **hand** represents “power” or “control.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [into the power of the ones seeking their life, and into the power of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the power of his servants]
See how you translated this phrase in 19:7.

In this verse, the word **she** is singular in form, but it refers to all the people of Egypt as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a plural form, as with **them** earlier in the verse. Alternate translation: [they will dwell]

Yahweh is using **as in the days of antiquity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as in former times.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as she did in former times]

27.q: אַל תִּירָ֞א עַבְדִּ֤⁠י יַֽעֲקֹב֙ וְ⁠אַל תֵּחַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל
27.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [do not be afraid at all, my servant Jacob, Israel]

27.q: אַל תִּירָ֞א עַבְדִּ֤⁠י יַֽעֲקֹב֙ וְ⁠אַל תֵּחַ֣ת
27.note: The words translated as **do not fear** and **nor be dismayed** are commands, but they communicate reassurance rather than a command. If these commands do not communicate reassurance for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates reassurance. Alternate translation: [there is no need for you to be afraid … nor any reason to be dismayed]
See how you translated “seed” in 7:15 where it is used with the same meaning.

The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing the people of Israel as if they were one person, **my servant Jacob**. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, **Jacob** represents “the descendants of Jacob,” that is, the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my servant, the descendants of Jacob]

27.q: וְ⁠שָׁ֧ב יַעֲק֛וֹב וְ⁠שָׁקַ֥ט וְ⁠שַׁאֲנַ֖ן וְ⁠אֵ֥ין מַחֲרִֽיד
27.note: Even though Yahweh is addressing the people of Israel directly, he is speaking of them in the third person as **Jacob**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [And you, people of Jacob, will return and will have quiet and will be at ease, and there will be no one making you afraid]

The terms **will have quiet** and **will be at ease** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and will live in complete peace]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:33.
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:10.
See how you translated the similar expression in 30:10.

28.note: SPEAKER is repeating forms of the verb **unpunished** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and I will certainly not leave you unpunished]

Yahweh is using **I am with you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will help and protect you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will help and protect you]

Yahweh says **all the nations** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [of the many nations where I have scattered you]

Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between what he will do to **all the nations** and what he will do to the people of Israel. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but as for you, I will not make a complete end of you]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And I will discipline you fairly]
See how you translated the similar expression in 46:27.
